claim: Fission yeast GATOR1 prevents deregulated activation of TORC1.
source: Previously, we identified fission yeast GATOR1 that prevents deregulated activation of TORC1 (Chia et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Chia et al., 2017).

claim: The GATOR2 subunit Sea3 is an ortholog of mammalian WDR59.
source: Unexpectedly, the GATOR2 subunit Sea3, an ortholog of mammalian WDR59, is physically and functionally proximal to GATOR1, rather than GATOR2, attenuating TORC1 activity.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the abstract and is based on sequence similarity and functional characterization presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sea3 is physically and functionally proximal to GATOR1, rather than GATOR2.
source: Unexpectedly, the GATOR2 subunit Sea3, an ortholog of mammalian WDR59, is physically and functionally proximal to GATOR1, rather than GATOR2, attenuating TORC1 activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and genetic analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sea3 attenuates TORC1 activity.
source: Unexpectedly, the GATOR2 subunit Sea3, an ortholog of mammalian WDR59, is physically and functionally proximal to GATOR1, rather than GATOR2, attenuating TORC1 activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic and biochemical data showing that loss of Sea3 leads to deregulated TORC1 activity.

claim: The fission yeast GATOR complex is dispensable for TORC1 regulation in response to amino acid starvation.
source: The fission yeast GATOR complex is dispensable for TORC1 regulation in response to amino acid starvation, which instead activates the Gcn2 pathway to inhibit TORC1 and induce autophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that GATOR1 mutants still respond to amino acid starvation through the Gcn2 pathway.

claim: Amino acid starvation activates the Gcn2 pathway to inhibit TORC1 and induce autophagy.
source: The fission yeast GATOR complex is dispensable for TORC1 regulation in response to amino acid starvation, which instead activates the Gcn2 pathway to inhibit TORC1 and induce autophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that Gcn2 mutants fail to inhibit TORC1 and induce autophagy during amino acid starvation.

claim: Nitrogen starvation suppresses TORC1 through the combined actions of the GATOR1-Sea3 complex, the Gcn2 pathway, and the TSC complex.
source: On the other hand, nitrogen starvation suppresses TORC1 through the combined actions of the GATOR1-Sea3 complex, the Gcn2 pathway, and the TSC complex, another conserved TORC1 inhibitor.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic and biochemical data showing that all three pathways contribute to TORC1 suppression during nitrogen starvation.

claim: Multiple, parallel signaling pathways implement negative regulation of TORC1 to ensure proper cellular starvation responses.
source: Thus, multiple, parallel signaling pathways implement negative regulation of TORC1 to ensure proper cellular starvation responses.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that GATOR1, Gcn2, and TSC complex function in parallel to regulate TORC1.

claim: TORC1 potentiates cellular anabolic processes including protein synthesis by phosphorylating ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein (4E-BP).
source: TORC1 potentiates cellular anabolic processes including protein synthesis by phosphorylating ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein (4E-BP) (Burnett et al., 1998; Ma and Blenis, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TORC1 inhibits the catabolic process autophagy by phosphorylating the components of the autophagy initiation complex.
source: On the other hand, TORC1 inhibits the catabolic process autophagy by phosphorylating the components of the autophagy initiation complex (Kamada et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2011; Puente et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Negative regulators of mammalian TORC1 (mTORC1) are frequently mutated in cancer cells.
source: Negative regulators of mammalian TORC1 (mTORC1) are frequently mutated in cancer cells and inhibition of mTORC1 effectively suppresses growth of some human cancers (Grabiner et al., 2014; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017; Shimobayashi and Hall, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inhibition of mTORC1 effectively suppresses growth of some human cancers.
source: Negative regulators of mammalian TORC1 (mTORC1) are frequently mutated in cancer cells and inhibition of mTORC1 effectively suppresses growth of some human cancers (Grabiner et al., 2014; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017; Shimobayashi and Hall, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In mammalian cells, the activity of mTORC1 is controlled on the lysosomal surface by the two types of small GTPases, Rheb and Rag.
source: In mammalian cells, the activity of mTORC1 is controlled on the lysosomal surface by the two types of small GTPases, Rheb and Rag.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: In its GTP-loaded state, Rheb activates mTORC1.
source: In its GTP-loaded state, Rheb activates mTORC1 (Saucedo et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2017), and this Rheb function is negatively regulated by the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) activity of the tumor-suppressing TSC complex composed of TSC1, TSC2, and TBC1D7 (Dibble et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Rheb function is negatively regulated by the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) activity of the tumor-suppressing TSC complex composed of TSC1, TSC2, and TBC1D7.
source: In its GTP-loaded state, Rheb activates mTORC1 (Saucedo et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2017), and this Rheb function is negatively regulated by the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) activity of the tumor-suppressing TSC complex composed of TSC1, TSC2, and TBC1D7 (Dibble et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the absence of growth factors or under energy stress, the TSC complex promotes the hydrolysis of GTP bound to Rheb, leading to mTORC1 inactivation.
source: In the absence of growth factors or under energy stress, the TSC complex promotes the hydrolysis of GTP bound to Rheb, leading to mTORC1 inactivation (Garami et al., 2003; Inoki et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Rag GTPases form a heterodimer of RagA or RagB bound to RagC or RagD.
source: The Rag GTPases form a heterodimer of RagA or RagB bound to RagC or RagD, which is anchored to the lysosomal membrane through a scaffold protein complex called Ragulator (Kim et al., 2008; Sancak et al., 2008; Sancak et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Rag heterodimer is anchored to the lysosomal membrane through a scaffold protein complex called Ragulator.
source: The Rag GTPases form a heterodimer of RagA or RagB bound to RagC or RagD, which is anchored to the lysosomal membrane through a scaffold protein complex called Ragulator (Kim et al., 2008; Sancak et al., 2008; Sancak et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the presence of amino acids, RagA/B becomes a GTP-loaded, active form and the Rag–Ragulator complex recruits mTORC1 to lysosomes, facilitating mTORC1 activation by Rheb.
source: In the presence of amino acids, RagA/B becomes a GTP-loaded, active form and the Rag–﻿Ragulator complex recruits mTORC1 to lysosomes, facilitating mTORC1 activation by Rheb.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: RagA/B is negatively regulated by its GAP complex GATOR1, which is composed of DEPDC5, Nprl2, and Nprl3.
source: RagA/B is negatively regulated by its GAP complex GATOR1 (GAP activity toward the Rag GTPases 1), which is composed of DEPDC5, Nprl2, and Nprl3 (Bar-Peled et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Amino acid stimuli inactivate the GAP activity of GATOR1 through its inhibitor GATOR2.
source: Amino acid stimuli inactivate the GAP activity of GATOR1 through its inhibitor GATOR2, a complex of the five proteins named WDR24, WDR59, MIOS, SEH1L, and SEC13, leading to an increase in GTP-bound RagA/B and thus, mTORC1 activation (Sancak et al., 2010; Bar-Peled et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GATOR2 is a complex of the five proteins named WDR24, WDR59, MIOS, SEH1L, and SEC13.
source: Amino acid stimuli inactivate the GAP activity of GATOR1 through its inhibitor GATOR2, a complex of the five proteins named WDR24, WDR59, MIOS, SEH1L, and SEC13, leading to an increase in GTP-bound RagA/B and thus, mTORC1 activation (Sancak et al., 2010; Bar-Peled et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The GATOR holocomplex composed of GATOR1 and GATOR2 serves as a conduit to transmit amino acid signals to mTORC1.
source: The GATOR holocomplex composed of GATOR1 and GATOR2 serves as a conduit to transmit amino acid signals to mTORC1.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Leucine and arginine are monitored by Sestrins and CASTOR1, respectively.
source: Leucine and arginine are monitored by Sestrins and CASTOR1, respectively, both of which bind and inhibit GATOR2 to inactivate mTORC1 when cells are starved of these amino acids (Chantranupong et al., 2016; Chantranupong et al., 2014; Parmigiani et al., 2014; Saxton et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sestrins and CASTOR1 bind and inhibit GATOR2 to inactivate mTORC1 when cells are starved of leucine and arginine.
source: Leucine and arginine are monitored by Sestrins and CASTOR1, respectively, both of which bind and inhibit GATOR2 to inactivate mTORC1 when cells are starved of these amino acids (Chantranupong et al., 2016; Chantranupong et al., 2014; Parmigiani et al., 2014; Saxton et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SAMTOR is a sensor for the methionine metabolite S-adenosylmethionine and mediates methionine-induced mTORC1 activation through GATOR1.
source: SAMTOR is a sensor for the methionine metabolite S-adenosylmethionine and mediates methionine-induced mTORC1 activation through GATOR1 (Gu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The mTORC1 subunits as well as the mTORC1 regulators such as the Rag GTPases, GATOR1, and GATOR2, are conserved from yeast to humans.
source: The mTORC1 subunits as well as the mTORC1 regulators described above, such as the Rag GTPases, GATOR1, and GATOR2, are conserved from yeast to humans (Tatebe and Shiozaki, 2017; Wolfson and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Gtr1–Gtr2 heterodimer, the SEACIT complex, and the SEACAT complex are the budding yeast counterparts of human RagA/B–RagC/D, GATOR1, and GATOR2, respectively.
source: The Gtr1–Gtr2 heterodimer, the SEACIT complex, and the SEACAT complex are the budding yeast counterparts of human RagA/B–RagC/D, GATOR1, and GATOR2, respectively (Dokudovskaya et al., 2011; Panchaud et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Ego1–Ego2–Ego3 complex is a Ragulator equivalent in budding yeast.
source: Based on the structural similarities, the Ego1–Ego2–Ego3 complex is a Ragulator equivalent in budding yeast, whereas no apparent Rheb and TSC orthologs are present in the TORC1 pathway of this yeast species (Kira et al., 2016; Powis et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: No apparent Rheb and TSC orthologs are present in the TORC1 pathway of budding yeast.
source: Based on the structural similarities, the Ego1–Ego2–Ego3 complex is a Ragulator equivalent in budding yeast, whereas no apparent Rheb and TSC orthologs are present in the TORC1 pathway of this yeast species (Kira et al., 2016; Powis et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In fission yeast, TORC1 is activated by the Rheb ortholog Rhb1.
source: In the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, another model eukaryote phylogenetically distant from budding yeast, TORC1 is activated by the Rheb ortholog Rhb1, which is under the negative regulation by the TSC complex as in mammalian cells (van Slegtenhorst et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Rhb1 is under the negative regulation by the TSC complex in fission yeast.
source: In the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, another model eukaryote phylogenetically distant from budding yeast, TORC1 is activated by the Rheb ortholog Rhb1, which is under the negative regulation by the TSC complex as in mammalian cells (van Slegtenhorst et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: TORC1 activity is attenuated by GATOR1 and Ragulator counterparts through the Rag GTPase heterodimer Gtr1–Gtr2 in S. pombe.
source: In addition, we previously identified GATOR1 and Ragulator counterparts in S. pombe and demonstrated that, even under nutrient-rich conditions, TORC1 activity is attenuated by these protein complexes through the Rag GTPase heterodimer Gtr1–Gtr2 (Chia et al., 2017; Fukuda and Shiozaki, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: The GATOR1 function can be replaced by the GDP-locked mutant form of Gtr1.
source: The GATOR1 function can be replaced by the GDP-locked mutant form of Gtr1, indicating that S. pombe GATOR1 functions as GAP for Gtr1.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: S. pombe GATOR1 functions as GAP for Gtr1.
source: The GATOR1 function can be replaced by the GDP-locked mutant form of Gtr1, indicating that S. pombe GATOR1 functions as GAP for Gtr1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic experiments showing that GDP-locked Gtr1 suppresses GATOR1 defects.

claim: Genetic experiments suggest that the negative regulation of TORC1 by the Gtr1–Gtr2 heterodimer is in parallel with that by the TSC complex.
source: Interestingly, genetic experiments suggest that the negative regulation of TORC1 by the Gtr1–Gtr2 heterodimer is in parallel with that by the TSC complex (Chia et al., 2017); thus, the Rag GTPases in S. pombe have an ability to regulate TORC1 independent of the Rheb GTPase.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The Rag GTPases in S. pombe have an ability to regulate TORC1 independent of the Rheb GTPase.
source: Interestingly, genetic experiments suggest that the negative regulation of TORC1 by the Gtr1–Gtr2 heterodimer is in parallel with that by the TSC complex (Chia et al., 2017); thus, the Rag GTPases in S. pombe have an ability to regulate TORC1 independent of the Rheb GTPase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic experiments showing parallel pathways.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis of GATOR1 purification detected Sea3, Sea4, Sec13, and Seh1 with sequence similarities to mammalian GATOR2 components.
source: In addition to Iml1 and Npr3 that constitute GATOR1, the analysis detected four additional proteins, Sea3, Sea4, Sec13, and Seh1, with sequence similarities to the mammalian GATOR2 components WDR59, MIOS, Sec13, and SEH1L, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Improved purification of GATOR1 identified Sea2, an ortholog of the mammalian GATOR2 subunit WDR24.
source: The GATOR1-interacting proteins included Sea2, an apparent ortholog of the mammalian GATOR2 subunit WDR24, in addition to the four other GATOR2 subunit orthologs that we previously detected (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All of the five subunits of GATOR2 appear to be conserved in fission yeast.
source: Thus, all of the five subunits of GATOR2 appear to be conserved in fission yeast and they form a complex with GATOR1 to constitute the GATOR holocomplex.
evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The five GATOR2 subunits form a complex with GATOR1 to constitute the GATOR holocomplex in fission yeast.
source: Thus, all of the five subunits of GATOR2 appear to be conserved in fission yeast and they form a complex with GATOR1 to constitute the GATOR holocomplex.
evidence: The claim is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Iml1 is localized to vacuolar membranes of fission yeast.
source: Iml1 is localized to vacuolar membranes of fission yeast (Chia et al., 2017), and consistently, the other GATOR1 subunits were also detected on vacuoles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The other GATOR1 subunits were also detected on vacuoles.
source: Iml1 is localized to vacuolar membranes of fission yeast (Chia et al., 2017), and consistently, the other GATOR1 subunits were also detected on vacuoles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sea2-GFP-mNG, Sea3-GFP-mNG, and Sea4-GFP are localized on vacuolar membranes.
source: Fluorescence microscopy detected Sea2-GFP-mNG, Sea3-GFP-mNG, and Sea4-GFP on vacuolar membranes that were illuminated by the FM4-64 dye (Figure 1D,E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figures 1D, E, and F.

claim: Seh1 was observed predominantly around the nuclear periphery, though weaker signals were also detectable on vacuoles.
source: Consistent with its role as a component of the nuclear pore complex (Baï et al., 2004), Seh1 was observed predominantly around the nuclear periphery, though weaker signals were also detectable on vacuoles (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1G and a citation.

claim: Together with GATOR1 and TORC1, GATOR2 resides on vacuoles.
source: These results are consistent with the notion that, together with GATOR1 and TORC1 (Chia et al., 2017), GATOR2 resides on vacuoles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from localization data and a citation.

claim: GFP-tagged Sec13 showed nuclear periphery signals and punctate fluorescence on the cell cortex.
source: As shown in Figure 1H, nuclear periphery signals and punctate fluorescence on the cell cortex were observed with GFP-tagged Sec13, which is known to function as a component of the nuclear pore complex as well as the vesicle coatomer COPII (Bilokapic and Schwartz, 2012; Pryer et al., 1993; Siniossoglou et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1H and citations.

claim: Only a small fraction of Sec13 might be in the GATOR2 complex on vacuoles.
source: Therefore, only a small fraction of Sec13 might be in the GATOR2 complex on vacuoles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localization pattern of Sec13.

claim: Loss of Sea3 results in a growth defect even in the presence of the other GATOR2 subunits.
source: On the other hand, cells lacking Sea3 exhibited significantly compromised growth both in the presence ('sea3∆' in Figure 2A) and absence ('sea3∆ seh1∆ sea2∆ sea4∆') of the other GATOR2 subunits.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The sea3∆ defect was suppressed by rapamycin in the growth medium.
source: Moreover, this sea3∆ defect was suppressed by rapamycin in the growth medium (Figure 2A, right), implying deregulated activation of TORC1 in cells lacking Sea3.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cells lacking Sea3 exhibit deregulated activation of TORC1.
source: Moreover, this sea3∆ defect was suppressed by rapamycin in the growth medium (Figure 2A, right), implying deregulated activation of TORC1 in cells lacking Sea3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rapamycin suppression of the sea3∆ growth defect.

claim: Among the GATOR2 components, Sea3 is likely to have a distinctive role in the negative regulation of TORC1 activity.
source: Thus, among the GATOR2 components, Sea3 is likely to have a distinctive role in the negative regulation of TORC1 activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the unique phenotype of sea3∆ compared to other GATOR2 mutants.

claim: Loss of Any1 rescues the growth defect of the sea3∆ and iml1∆ mutants.
source: Another similarity between the sea3∆ mutant and the GATOR1 mutants such as iml1∆ is that their growth defects are complemented by the loss of Any1 (Figure 2B), an inhibitor of the plasma membrane localization of amino acid permeases (Nakase et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2B and a citation.

claim: Together with the known GATOR1 components, Sea3 appears to suppress deregulated TORC1 activation that impedes cellular amino acid uptake.
source: Therefore, together with the known GATOR1 components, Sea3 appears to suppress deregulated TORC1 activation that impedes cellular amino acid uptake (Chia et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the any1∆ suppression phenotype and a citation.

claim: The growth defects of the strains lacking the GATOR1 components (iml1∆, npr2∆, and npr3∆) were not exacerbated by the sea3∆ mutation.
source: In accordance with our hypothesis, the growth defects of the strains lacking the GATOR1 components (iml1∆, npr2∆, and npr3∆) were not exacerbated by the sea3∆ mutation (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The sea3∆ tsc1∆ and sea3∆ tsc2∆ double mutants exhibited severe growth defects suppressible by rapamycin.
source: On the contrary, the sea3∆ tsc1∆ and sea3∆ tsc2∆ double mutants exhibited severe growth defects suppressible by rapamycin (Figure 2D), indicating that, like GATOR1 (Chia et al., 2017), Sea3 attenuates TORC1 activity independent of the TSC complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Like GATOR1, Sea3 attenuates TORC1 activity independent of the TSC complex.
source: On the contrary, the sea3∆ tsc1∆ and sea3∆ tsc2∆ double mutants exhibited severe growth defects suppressible by rapamycin (Figure 2D), indicating that, like GATOR1 (Chia et al., 2017), Sea3 attenuates TORC1 activity independent of the TSC complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the synthetic growth defect and a citation.

claim: The loss of Sea3 was complemented by the gtr1S16N allele.
source: Furthermore, the loss of Sea3 was complemented by the gtr1S16N allele ('gtr1SN' in Figure 2E), which expresses the GDP-locked mutant form of the Gtr1 GTPase, suggesting that the function of GATOR1 as Gtr1 GAP is compromised in the absence of Sea3.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The function of GATOR1 as Gtr1 GAP is compromised in the absence of Sea3.
source: Furthermore, the loss of Sea3 was complemented by the gtr1S16N allele ('gtr1SN' in Figure 2E), which expresses the GDP-locked mutant form of the Gtr1 GTPase, suggesting that the function of GATOR1 as Gtr1 GAP is compromised in the absence of Sea3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic suppression by GDP-locked Gtr1.

claim: In wild-type cells, the phosphorylation of Psk1 disappeared within 20 min after nitrogen starvation.
source: In wild-type cells, the phosphorylation of Psk1 disappeared within 20 min after nitrogen starvation, which promptly inactivates TORC1 in fission yeast (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The Psk1 phosphorylation in the sea3∆ mutant was detectable even after 30 min of nitrogen starvation.
source: The Psk1 phosphorylation in the sea3∆ mutant, however, was detectable even after 30 min of nitrogen starvation, indicating deregulated TORC1 activity that lacks an expeditious response to the nutrient.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Dephosphorylation of Psk1 after the starvation in sea3∆ cells was not delayed as much as in iml1∆ cells.
source: Consistent with the sea3∆ phenotype being less severe than that of iml1∆ (Figure 2B,C and E), dephosphorylation of Psk1 after the starvation in sea3∆ cells was not delayed as much as in iml1∆ cells (Figure 2G); therefore, GATOR1 appears to be partially active even in the absence of Sea3.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: GATOR1 appears to be partially active even in the absence of Sea3.
source: Consistent with the sea3∆ phenotype being less severe than that of iml1∆ (Figure 2B,C and E), dephosphorylation of Psk1 after the starvation in sea3∆ cells was not delayed as much as in iml1∆ cells (Figure 2G); therefore, GATOR1 appears to be partially active even in the absence of Sea3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of Psk1 dephosphorylation kinetics.

claim: Cells lacking the other GATOR2 components (seh1∆ sea2∆ sea4∆) displayed starvation-induced Psk1 dephosphorylation comparable to that in wild-type cells.
source: On the other hand, cells lacking the other GATOR2 components (seh1∆ sea2∆ sea4∆) displayed starvation-induced Psk1 dephosphorylation comparable to that in wild-type cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Sea3 promotes the GATOR1 function, which attenuates TORC1 signaling as GAP for the Gtr1 GTPase.
source: Taken together, these data strongly suggest that Sea3, a fission yeast ortholog of the mammalian GATOR2 subunit WDR59, promotes the GATOR1 function, which attenuates TORC1 signaling as GAP for the Gtr1 GTPase.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of genetic and biochemical evidence.

claim: Sea3 is required for the interaction between Iml1 and the other GATOR2 components Seh1, Sea2, Sea4, and Sec13.
source: Immunoprecipitation of the GATOR1 subunit Iml1 from the sea3+ and sea3∆ cell lysates revealed that Sea3 is required for the interaction between Iml1 and the other GATOR2 components Seh1 (Figure 3A), Sea2 (Figure 3B), Sea4 (Figure 3C), and Sec13 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figures 3A-D.

claim: Iml1 and Sea3 were co-immunoprecipitated even in the absence of Seh1, Sea2, and Sea4.
source: On the other hand, Iml1 and Sea3 were co-immunoprecipitated even in the absence of Seh1, Sea2, and Sea4 (Figure 3E), implying that Sea3 directly binds to GATOR1 and anchors the other GATOR2 components to GATOR1.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Sea3 directly binds to GATOR1 and anchors the other GATOR2 components to GATOR1.
source: On the other hand, Iml1 and Sea3 were co-immunoprecipitated even in the absence of Seh1, Sea2, and Sea4 (Figure 3E), implying that Sea3 directly binds to GATOR1 and anchors the other GATOR2 components to GATOR1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The binding of Sea3 to GATOR1 is dependent on the integrity of the GATOR1 complex.
source: The binding of Sea3 to GATOR1 is dependent on the integrity of the GATOR1 complex, and the absence of any one of the GATOR1 subunits disrupted the Sea3–GATOR1 association (Figure 3F,G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figures 3F, G, and H.

claim: In the absence of intact GATOR1, the vacuolar localization of Sea3 was lost and the protein diffused throughout the cytosol.
source: Consistently, in the absence of intact GATOR1, the vacuolar localization of Sea3 (Figure 1E) was lost and the protein diffused throughout the cytosol (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Sea3 is localized to vacuolar membranes through its interaction with GATOR1.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sea3 is localized to vacuolar membranes through its interaction with GATOR1.
source: Consistently, in the absence of intact GATOR1, the vacuolar localization of Sea3 (Figure 1E) was lost and the protein diffused throughout the cytosol (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Sea3 is localized to vacuolar membranes through its interaction with GATOR1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localization defect in GATOR1 mutants.

claim: Deregulated TORC1 activation in the absence of functional GATOR1 per se does not cause the Sea3 diffusion in the cytosol.
source: It should be noted that deregulated TORC1 activation in the absence of functional GATOR1 per se does not cause the Sea3 diffusion in the cytosol (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B); vacuolar localization of Sea3 was observed in cells expressing the GTP-locked Gtr1Q61L mutant protein, which induces TORC1 hyper-activation by mimicking the GATOR1 defect (Chia et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and a citation.

claim: The vacuolar localization of Sea2, Sea4, and Seh1 was abrogated in the sea3∆ background.
source: Furthermore, consistent with the essential role of Sea3 in the interaction between GATOR1 and the other GATOR2 subunits, the vacuolar localization of Sea2, Sea4, and Seh1 (Figure 1D,F and G) was abrogated in the sea3∆ background (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Sea3 plays an essential role in the assembly of the GATOR holocomplex by mediating the association of the GATOR2 components with GATOR1 on the vacuolar surface.
source: These results strongly suggest that Sea3 plays an essential role in the assembly of the GATOR holocomplex by mediating the association of the GATOR2 components with GATOR1 on the vacuolar surface.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from localization and interaction data.

claim: Sea3 is not essential for the integrity of the GATOR1 complex.
source: Immunoblotting experiments detected no significant difference between wild-type and sea3∆ cells in the cellular levels of the GATOR1 components Iml1, Npr2, and Npr3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A). In addition, the pairwise interactions among the GATOR1 subunits were confirmed by immunoprecipitation experiments with the cell lysate from the sea3∆ strains (Figure 3J,K and L), suggesting that Sea3 is not essential for the assembly of the GATOR1 complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting and co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Figures 3J, K, and L.

claim: Sea3 is dispensable for the vacuolar localization of GATOR1.
source: In the case of the sea3∆ mutant, Iml1, Npr2, and Npr3 were all detectable on vacuoles (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F and G), indicating that Sea3 is dispensable for the vacuolar localization of GATOR1.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, F, and G.

claim: The physical interaction between GATOR1 and the Gtr1 GTPase was reduced in the sea3∆ mutant.
source: On the other hand, immunoprecipitation of the GATOR1 subunit Iml1 found that the physical interaction between GATOR1 and the Gtr1 GTPase was reduced in the sea3∆ mutant (Figure 3M).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Sea3 facilitates the GAP function of GATOR1 by promoting or stabilizing the physical interaction between GATOR1 and the Gtr1 GTPase.
source: This result raises the possibility that Sea3 facilitates the GAP function of GATOR1 by promoting or stabilizing the physical interaction between GATOR1 and the Gtr1 GTPase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced interaction between GATOR1 and Gtr1 in the absence of Sea3.

claim: Arg854 of S. pombe Iml1 is not essential for the GATOR1 function.
source: The new, confirmed iml1R854A strain showed no apparent growth defect (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), indicating that Arg854 of S. pombe Iml1 is not essential for the GATOR1 function.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Arg78 of mammalian Nprl2 was proposed to serve as an arginine finger that promotes GTP hydrolysis by RagA/B.
source: Recently, another conserved arginine residue in mammalian GATOR1, Arg78 of the Nprl2 subunit, was proposed to serve as an arginine finger that promotes GTP hydrolysis by RagA/B (Shen et al., 2019, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The npr2R98A mutant cells exhibited a compromised growth phenotype that was rescued by rapamycin or the gtr1SN mutation.
source: The mutant cells exhibited a compromised growth phenotype that was rescued by rapamycin or the gtr1SN mutation, an indicative of compromised GAP activity of GATOR1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The conserved Arg residue in Npr2, but not the one in Iml1, acts as an arginine finger of GATOR1 in fission yeast.
source: Though the npr2R98A phenotype was not as severe as that of the npr2 null mutant, these observations are in line with the model that the conserved Arg residue in Npr2, but not the one in Iml1, acts as an arginine finger of GATOR1 also in fission yeast.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of npr2R98A and iml1R854A phenotypes.

claim: Autophagic degradation of GFP-tagged phosphoglycerate kinase (Pgk1) has been successfully used as a quantitative readout of autophagy.
source: Autophagic degradation of GFP-tagged phosphoglycerate kinase (Pgk1) has been successfully used as a quantitative readout of autophagy (Welter et al., 2010; Fukuda et al., 2020); upon autophagy induction, Pgk1-GFP is transported from the cytoplasm to vacuoles for degradation, but the GFP moiety remains undigested due to its resistance to the vacuolar proteases.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Upon autophagy induction, Pgk1-GFP is transported from the cytoplasm to vacuoles for degradation, but the GFP moiety remains undigested due to its resistance to the vacuolar proteases.
source: Autophagic degradation of GFP-tagged phosphoglycerate kinase (Pgk1) has been successfully used as a quantitative readout of autophagy (Welter et al., 2010; Fukuda et al., 2020); upon autophagy induction, Pgk1-GFP is transported from the cytoplasm to vacuoles for degradation, but the GFP moiety remains undigested due to its resistance to the vacuolar proteases.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the Pgk1-GFP autophagy assay.

claim: No accumulation of GFP was detected in cells lacking Atg7 or the vacuolar protease Isp6.
source: As expected, no accumulation of GFP was detected in cells lacking Atg7, a core autophagy regulator, or the vacuolar protease Isp6 (Kohda et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation.

claim: The tsc2∆ and iml1∆ strains exhibited only partial reduction in the amounts of released GFP during nitrogen starvation.
source: Using this assay, we examined the nitrogen starvation-induced autophagy in the tsc2∆ and iml1∆ strains, both of which exhibited only partial reduction in the amounts of released GFP (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Autophagy was still detectable in the tsc2∆ iml1∆ double mutant during nitrogen starvation.
source: Though much less than that in wild-type cells, autophagy was still detectable in the tsc2∆ iml1∆ double mutant, indicating that, in addition to the GATOR1 and TSC complexes, there must be an additional mechanism to attenuate TORC1 upon nitrogen starvation for autophagy induction.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In addition to the GATOR1 and TSC complexes, there must be an additional mechanism to attenuate TORC1 upon nitrogen starvation for autophagy induction.
source: Though much less than that in wild-type cells, autophagy was still detectable in the tsc2∆ iml1∆ double mutant, indicating that, in addition to the GATOR1 and TSC complexes, there must be an additional mechanism to attenuate TORC1 upon nitrogen starvation for autophagy induction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the residual autophagy in the tsc2∆ iml1∆ double mutant.

claim: The Gcn2 protein kinase is activated in response to amino acid starvation and phosphorylates eIF2α to induce the general amino acid control response.
source: The Gcn2 protein kinase is activated in response to amino acid starvation and phosphorylates eIF2α to induce the general amino acid control response (Zhan et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Leucine starvation induced Gcn2 activation, which was monitored by immunoblotting to detect phosphorylated eIF2α.
source: Such leucine starvation induced Gcn2 activation, which was monitored by immunoblotting to detect phosphorylated eIF2α (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When cells expressing Pgk1-GFP were starved of leucine, free GFP accumulated, though more slowly than in cells starved of nitrogen.
source: When cells expressing Pgk1-GFP were starved of leucine, free GFP accumulated, though more slowly than in cells starved of nitrogen (Figure 4B); thus, leucine starvation induces autophagy in S. pombe.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Leucine starvation induces autophagy in S. pombe.
source: When cells expressing Pgk1-GFP were starved of leucine, free GFP accumulated, though more slowly than in cells starved of nitrogen (Figure 4B); thus, leucine starvation induces autophagy in S. pombe.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No GFP accumulation was detected in gcn2∆ cells under leucine starvation.
source: However, no GFP accumulation was detected in gcn2∆ cells under leucine starvation (Figure 4C), demonstrating that the autophagy induced by leucine starvation is dependent on the Gcn2 kinase.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The autophagy induced by leucine starvation is dependent on the Gcn2 kinase.
source: However, no GFP accumulation was detected in gcn2∆ cells under leucine starvation (Figure 4C), demonstrating that the autophagy induced by leucine starvation is dependent on the Gcn2 kinase.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In cells of arginine auxotrophy, Gcn2-dependent autophagy was detectable after incubation in the growth medium without arginine.
source: Similarly, in cells of arginine auxotrophy, Gcn2-dependent autophagy was detectable after incubation in the growth medium without arginine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Gcn2-dependent induction of autophagy was observed in cells treated by 3-amino-1,2,4-triazole (3-AT) or methionine sulfoximine (MSX).
source: Gcn2-dependent induction of autophagy was also observed in cells treated by 3-amino-1,2,4-triazole (3-AT) or methionine sulfoximine (MSX), inhibitors of histidine and glutamine biosynthesis, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Autophagy can be induced in fission yeast cells starved of various amino acids in a Gcn2-dependent manner.
source: These observations collectively indicate that autophagy can be induced in fission yeast cells starved of various amino acids in a Gcn2-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple autophagy experiments with different amino acid starvation conditions.

claim: The loss of Hri1 and Hri2, two other eIF2α kinases in S. pombe, did not affect autophagy after leucine starvation.
source: By contrast, the loss of Hri1 and Hri2, two other eIF2α kinases in S. pombe (Zhan et al., 2004), did not affect autophagy after leucine starvation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), indicating that Gcn2 exclusively regulates the leucine starvation-induced autophagy among the S. pombe eIF2α kinases.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and a citation.

claim: Gcn2 exclusively regulates the leucine starvation-induced autophagy among the S. pombe eIF2α kinases.
source: By contrast, the loss of Hri1 and Hri2, two other eIF2α kinases in S. pombe (Zhan et al., 2004), did not affect autophagy after leucine starvation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), indicating that Gcn2 exclusively regulates the leucine starvation-induced autophagy among the S. pombe eIF2α kinases.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of effect of Hri1 and Hri2 deletion on leucine starvation-induced autophagy.

claim: The Gcn2 kinase forms a complex with the Gcn1 and Gcn20 proteins that facilitate activation of Gcn2.
source: The Gcn2 kinase forms a complex with the Gcn1 and Gcn20 proteins that facilitate activation of Gcn2 (Garcia-Barrio et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Autophagy in response to leucine starvation was abrogated by the gcn1∆, but not gcn20∆, mutation.
source: Autophagy in response to leucine starvation was abrogated by the gcn1∆, but not gcn20∆, mutation (Figure 4D), consistent with the fact that Gcn1 directly regulates Gcn2, but Gcn20 has only a minor role in Gcn2 signaling (Sattlegger et al., 2004; Yuan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4D and citations.

claim: Autophagy after leucine starvation was severely impaired in cells lacking Cpc2 and in those overexpressing a fission yeast ortholog of Yih1/IMPACT.
source: We found that autophagy after leucine starvation was severely impaired in cells lacking Cpc2 and in those overexpressing a fission yeast ortholog of Yih1/IMPACT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), confirming the essential role of the Gcn2 activity in autophagy induction upon amino acid starvation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The eIF2α-S52A strain was defective in the leucine starvation-induced autophagy.
source: In order to test whether the Gcn2 kinase induces autophagy through phosphorylation of eIF2α, we constructed a strain that expresses eIF2α with its phosphorylation site Ser52 substituted by alanine (eIF2α-S52A). The strain was defective in the leucine starvation-induced autophagy (Figure 4E), indicating the critical role of the eIF2α phosphorylation by Gcn2.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The eIF2α phosphorylation by Gcn2 plays a critical role in leucine starvation-induced autophagy.
source: In order to test whether the Gcn2 kinase induces autophagy through phosphorylation of eIF2α, we constructed a strain that expresses eIF2α with its phosphorylation site Ser52 substituted by alanine (eIF2α-S52A). The strain was defective in the leucine starvation-induced autophagy (Figure 4E), indicating the critical role of the eIF2α phosphorylation by Gcn2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the autophagy defect in the eIF2α-S52A mutant.

claim: After leucine starvation, the Fil1 protein increased, which was dependent on Gcn2 and the phosphorylation of eIF2α.
source: Indeed, we observed that, after leucine starvation, the Fil1 protein increased, which was dependent on Gcn2 and the phosphorylation of eIF2α (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: S. pombe cells lacking Gcn3 or Fil1 displayed autophagy defects during leucine starvation.
source: Moreover, S. pombe cells lacking Gcn3 (Figure 4D) or Fil1 (Figure 4F) displayed autophagy defects during leucine starvation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: Activation of the transcriptional program induced by the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway promotes autophagy in response to amino acid starvation.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that activation of the transcriptional program induced by the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway promotes autophagy in response to amino acid starvation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence showing the requirement of Gcn2, eIF2α phosphorylation, and Fil1 for autophagy.

claim: When fission yeast cells were starved of leucine, the TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Psk1 became undetectable.
source: When fission yeast cells were starved of leucine, the TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Psk1 became undetectable, indicating that TORC1 activity is suppressed upon leucine starvation (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: TORC1 activity is suppressed upon leucine starvation.
source: When fission yeast cells were starved of leucine, the TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Psk1 became undetectable, indicating that TORC1 activity is suppressed upon leucine starvation (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the loss of Psk1 phosphorylation during leucine starvation.

claim: Psk1 remained phosphorylated even after leucine starvation in the gcn2∆, eIF2α-S52A, and fil1∆ mutant strains.
source: In contrast, Psk1 remained phosphorylated even after the starvation in the gcn2∆, eIF2α-S52A, and fil1∆ mutant strains (Figure 5A), suggesting that TORC1 inactivation in leucine-starved cells is mediated by the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: TORC1 inactivation in leucine-starved cells is mediated by the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway.
source: In contrast, Psk1 remained phosphorylated even after the starvation in the gcn2∆, eIF2α-S52A, and fil1∆ mutant strains (Figure 5A), suggesting that TORC1 inactivation in leucine-starved cells is mediated by the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the persistence of Psk1 phosphorylation in Gcn2 pathway mutants.

claim: The autophagy defect of the gcn2∆ mutant was complemented by TORC1 inactivation by the TORC1 inhibitors, rapamycin and caffeine.
source: Moreover, the autophagy defect of the gcn2∆ mutant was complemented by TORC1 inactivation by the TORC1 inhibitors, rapamycin and caffeine (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Gcn2 pathway attenuates TORC1 activity in response to amino acid starvation to induce autophagy.
source: These results suggest that the Gcn2 pathway attenuates TORC1 activity in response to amino acid starvation to induce autophagy.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the rescue of gcn2∆ autophagy defect by TORC1 inhibitors.

claim: The strains lacking the functional TSC or GATOR1 complex showed no apparent defect in amino acid starvation-induced autophagy.
source: In stark contrast to the Gcn2 pathway mutants, the strains lacking the functional TSC or GATOR1 complex showed no apparent defect in amino acid starvation-induced autophagy; free GFP, the product of the autophagic degradation of Pgk1-GFP, accumulated after leucine starvation even in the tsc2∆ iml1∆ double mutant (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Amino acid starvation can induce autophagy independent of the TSC and GATOR1 complexes.
source: Thus, amino acid starvation can induce autophagy independent of the TSC and GATOR1 complexes, two important negative regulators of TORC1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal autophagy in tsc2∆ iml1∆ cells during leucine starvation.

claim: Significant autophagy induction was observed in gcn2∆, eIF2α-S52A, and fil1∆ cells incubated in the growth medium with no nitrogen source.
source: On the other hand, we observed significant autophagy induction in gcn2∆ (Figure 5D), eIF2α-S52A, and fil1∆ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) cells incubated in the growth medium with no nitrogen source.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nitrogen depletion triggered TORC1 inactivation in Gcn2 pathway mutants as in the wild-type strain.
source: Consistently, nitrogen depletion triggered TORC1 inactivation in these Gcn2 pathway mutants as in the wild-type strain (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The Gcn2 signaling pathway appears to be specifically responsible for induction of autophagy in response to amino acid starvation.
source: Therefore, the Gcn2 signaling pathway appears to be specifically responsible for induction of autophagy in response to amino acid starvation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential requirement of Gcn2 for autophagy during amino acid versus nitrogen starvation.

claim: The Gcn2-dependent phosphorylation of eIF2α and the Fil1 expression increased more significantly during starvation for leucine than that for nitrogen.
source: Such a specific role of the Gcn2 pathway during amino acid starvation is also congruous with our observation that the Gcn2-dependent phosphorylation of eIF2α and the Fil1 expression increased more significantly during starvation for leucine than that for nitrogen (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ double-mutant cells starved of nitrogen, autophagy was severely reduced and delayed, in comparison to those in the wild-type and individual single-mutant cells.
source: In the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ double-mutant cells starved of nitrogen, autophagy was severely reduced and delayed, in comparison to those in the wild-type and individual single-mutant cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The autophagy defect in the gcn2∆ iml1∆ double mutant was even more severe than that in the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ double mutant.
source: The autophagy defect in the gcn2∆ iml1∆ double mutant was even more severe than that in the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ double mutant (Figure 6B,C), implying that GATOR1 and Gcn2 are two main contributors to the nitrogen starvation-induced autophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: GATOR1 and Gcn2 are two main contributors to the nitrogen starvation-induced autophagy.
source: The autophagy defect in the gcn2∆ iml1∆ double mutant was even more severe than that in the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ double mutant (Figure 6B,C), implying that GATOR1 and Gcn2 are two main contributors to the nitrogen starvation-induced autophagy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of autophagy defects in different double mutants.

claim: In the gnc2∆ iml1∆ tsc2∆ triple mutant, a trace of released GFP was detected only after 14 hr of nitrogen starvation.
source: In the gnc2∆ iml1∆ tsc2∆ triple mutant, a trace of released GFP was detected only after 14 hr of nitrogen starvation (Figure 6C), while autophagy takes place within 2 hr in wild-type cells after the starvation (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Autophagy induction upon nitrogen starvation is dependent on the three negative regulators of TORC1 signaling, GATOR1, Gcn2, and the TSC complex.
source: These data indicate that autophagy induction upon nitrogen starvation is dependent on the three negative regulators of TORC1 signaling, GATOR1, Gcn2, and the TSC complex.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the severe autophagy defect in the triple mutant.

claim: In strains lacking GATOR1, Gcn2, and the TSC complex, severely impaired suppression of TORC1 activity during nitrogen starvation was confirmed by monitoring the TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Psk1.
source: Not surprisingly, in strains lacking these regulators, severely impaired suppression of TORC1 activity during nitrogen starvation was confirmed by monitoring the TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Psk1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The gcn2∆ iml1∆ double mutant exhibited a significant delay in the nitrogen starvation-responsive TORC1 inactivation.
source: Especially, the gcn2∆ iml1∆ double mutant exhibited a significant delay in the nitrogen starvation-responsive TORC1 inactivation, consistent with its severe defect in autophagy induction (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The gcn2∆ iml1∆ tsc2∆ triple mutant showed robust Psk1 phosphorylation even after 12 hr of nitrogen starvation.
source: With a more severe autophagy phenotype (Figure 6C), the gcn2∆ iml1∆ tsc2∆ triple mutant showed robust Psk1 phosphorylation even after 12 hr of nitrogen starvation (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Nitrogen starvation provoked significant eIF2α phosphorylation in the GATOR1- and TSC-defective strains, but not in the wild type.
source: Indeed, nitrogen starvation provoked significant eIF2α phosphorylation in the GATOR1- and TSC-defective strains, but not in the wild type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B); the loss of the GATOR1 and TSC complexes may be compensated by activation of the Gcn2 kinase to attenuate TORC1.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The loss of the GATOR1 and TSC complexes may be compensated by activation of the Gcn2 kinase to attenuate TORC1.
source: Indeed, nitrogen starvation provoked significant eIF2α phosphorylation in the GATOR1- and TSC-defective strains, but not in the wild type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B); the loss of the GATOR1 and TSC complexes may be compensated by activation of the Gcn2 kinase to attenuate TORC1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased eIF2α phosphorylation in GATOR1 and TSC mutants.

claim: Nitrogen starvation induced significant Gcn2 activation in autophagy-defective mutants, such as atg7∆ and isp6∆, more than in wild-type cells.
source: Nitrogen starvation also induced significant Gcn2 activation in autophagy-defective mutants, such as atg7∆ and isp6∆, more than in wild-type cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), implying that autophagy suppresses Gcn2 activation during nitrogen starvation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Autophagy suppresses Gcn2 activation during nitrogen starvation.
source: Nitrogen starvation also induced significant Gcn2 activation in autophagy-defective mutants, such as atg7∆ and isp6∆, more than in wild-type cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), implying that autophagy suppresses Gcn2 activation during nitrogen starvation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased Gcn2 activation in autophagy-defective mutants.

claim: Reduced autophagy in the absence of the GATOR1 and TSC complexes after nitrogen starvation may lead to intracellular amino acid depletion, which induces Gcn2 activation via uncharged tRNAs.
source: It is plausible that reduced autophagy in the absence of the GATOR1 and TSC complexes after nitrogen starvation (Figure 4A) may lead to intracellular amino acid depletion, which induces Gcn2 activation via uncharged tRNAs (Wek et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the relationship between autophagy and Gcn2 activation, supported by a citation.

claim: Autophagy became detectable 2–3 hr after nitrogen starvation in the iml1∆ tsc2∆ strain.
source: Autophagy became detectable 2–3 hr after nitrogen starvation in the iml1∆ tsc2∆ strain, and much later in the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant, while gcn2∆ iml1∆ cells showed only minuscule autophagy signals even after 9 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The reduction in TORC1 activity was observed early after the starvation in the iml1∆ tsc2∆ mutant, followed by the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant, and then the gcn2∆ iml1∆ strain.
source: Consistently, the reduction in TORC1 activity, as judged by Psk1 dephosphorylation, was also observed early after the starvation in the iml1∆ tsc2∆ mutant, followed by the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant, and then the gcn2∆ iml1∆ strain (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Gcn2 signaling contributes the most to TORC1 attenuation during nitrogen starvation, whereas the TSC complex does the least among the three.
source: These observations may reflect the contributions of the three negative regulators of TORC1 during nitrogen starvation; Gcn2 signaling contributes the most, whereas the TSC complex does the least among the three.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the kinetics of autophagy and TORC1 inactivation in different mutants.

claim: The gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant with functional GATOR1 exhibited a transient reduction in TORC1 activity within 1 hr of nitrogen starvation.
source: Of note, the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant with functional GATOR1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E,F), but not the gcn2∆ iml1∆ tsc2∆ triple mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F), exhibited a transient reduction in TORC1 activity within 1 hr of nitrogen starvation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: GATOR1 can attenuate TORC1 promptly after nitrogen starvation, but negative feedback regulation that re-activates TORC1 or inhibits GATOR1 might be induced in response to the TORC1 attenuation.
source: Therefore, it seems that GATOR1 can attenuate TORC1 promptly after the starvation, but negative feedback regulation that re-activates TORC1 or inhibits GATOR1 might be induced in response to the TORC1 attenuation.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the transient TORC1 inactivation in the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant.

claim: The GATOR1-dependent TORC1 attenuation preceded the Gcn2-mediated TORC1 inhibition, which became apparent after 2 hr of nitrogen starvation.
source: This GATOR1-dependent TORC1 attenuation preceded the Gcn2-mediated TORC1 inhibition, which became apparent after 2 hr of the starvation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Together with GATOR1, the TSC complex may be able to initiate the suppression of TORC1 activity much earlier than the Gcn2 pathway after nitrogen starvation.
source: In addition, in the gcn2∆ single mutant that retains both GATOR1 and the TSC complex, a notable reduction in TORC1 activity was observed even earlier, within 10 min after the starvation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G). Thus, together with GATOR1, the TSC complex may be able to initiate the suppression of TORC1 activity much earlier than the Gcn2 pathway after nitrogen starvation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the early TORC1 inactivation in the gcn2∆ mutant.

claim: The relatively late contribution of Gcn2 to TORC1 attenuation in starved cells can be explained by the fact that Gcn2 functions through the Fil1-mediated transcriptional events.
source: The relatively late contribution of Gcn2 to TORC1 attenuation in starved cells can be explained by the fact that Gcn2 functions through the Fil1-mediated transcriptional events.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the mechanism of Gcn2 action.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation and Fil1 up-regulation were detectable as early as at 15 min after nitrogen starvation.
source: Indeed, eIF2α phosphorylation and Fil1 up-regulation were detectable as early as at 15 min after the starvation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2H), whereas the Gcn2-dependent TORC1 inactivation took place after 2 hr and later (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2H.

claim: The tsc1∆ and tsc2∆ mutants show no apparent growth defect, but introduction of the gcn2∆ mutation to them resulted in a detectable growth defect.
source: The tsc1∆ and tsc2∆ mutants show no apparent growth defect, but introduction of the gcn2∆ mutation to them resulted in a detectable growth defect (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The gcn2∆ mutation exacerbated the growth defects in cells lacking functional GATOR1 or Sea3.
source: In addition, the gcn2∆ mutation exacerbated the growth defects in cells lacking functional GATOR1 (Figure 6G) or Sea3 (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figures 6G and 6H.

claim: Not only gcn2∆ but also fil1∆ exhibited similar synthetic growth defects when combined with the tsc2∆ or sea3∆ mutation.
source: Not only gcn2∆ but also fil1∆ exhibited similar synthetic growth defects when combined with the tsc2∆ (Figure 6I) or sea3∆ (Figure 6J) mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figures 6I and 6J.

claim: Growth phenotypes caused by the Gcn2 pathway mutations combined with the loss of the other negative regulators of TORC1 were largely suppressed by rapamycin in the growth medium or by the any1∆ mutation.
source: Importantly, these growth phenotypes caused by the Gcn2 pathway mutations combined with the loss of the other negative regulators of TORC1 were largely suppressed by rapamycin in the growth medium (right panels in Figure 6F–J) or by the any1∆ mutation (Figure 6K).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figures 6F-K.

claim: Along with the TSC and GATOR1 complexes, the Gcn2 signaling pathway also contributes to TORC1 attenuation in the presence of ample nutrients.
source: Thus, it is likely that, along with the TSC and GATOR1 complexes, the Gcn2 signaling pathway also contributes to TORC1 attenuation in the presence of ample nutrients.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the synthetic growth defects and their suppression by rapamycin or any1∆.

claim: iml1∆ and tsc2∆ cells starved of nitrogen gradually lost viability.
source: We also noticed that iml1∆ and tsc2∆ cells starved of nitrogen gradually lost viability, though such a phenotype was not detectable with the gcn2∆ mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Significantly reduced mating and sporulation were observed in strains carrying the iml1∆ mutation.
source: Significantly reduced mating and sporulation were observed in strains carrying the iml1∆ mutation, suggesting an important role of GATOR1 in the induction of sexual differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mating and sporulation assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: GATOR1 plays an important role in the induction of sexual differentiation.
